implementation_notes: Ruby's load semantics are the eager mechanism: require executes a file's top-level code once and returns the same result afterwards, so the conventional realisation is acquisition at load time - a file whose body opens the pool, client or connection - or an explicit warm-up call in a boot file. Ruby makes the eager/lazy choice unusually visible in its concurrency library: Concurrent::Promise is created unscheduled and the work begins when it is executed/posted (Promise.execute starts it immediately), while keeping the work behind an accessor that runs it on demand is the lazy form. Because load-time acquisition has no natural owner, pair it with an explicit release (at_exit or a shutdown hook) or the resource outlives the code that created it.
code_sketch:
# config/initializers/resources.rb - required once, before serving
DB = Sequel.connect(url, max_connections: 8)
DB.test_connection                     # validate eagerly
at_exit { DB.disconnect }              # explicit owner for release

# eager vs deferred in one library:
#   Concurrent::Promise.execute { ... }  starts now
#   an accessor that runs the work on first use  is lazy
pitfalls: require order decides what exists: a file that acquires at load time and depends on another initializer sees an unloaded constant (NameError) or a half-configured one.
Eagerly opened connections and threads are inherited across fork in preforking servers (Puma, Unicorn), so each child must reconnect instead of sharing the parent's socket.
Code-reloading setups (Rails reloaders) replace constants while threads started eagerly at load keep references to the replaced objects, producing stale-class bugs.
